title: Cap. VIII Resp.: election and praeterition from mere good pleasure; those passed by were children of wrath
pass_a_gloss: Further, in electing or passing by he does not regard any external circumstance of nation, of nobility, or anything similar, but acts from the mere good pleasure of his will. Finally, those whom he passes by cannot pretend that they feared God and lived justly, but are compelled on the contrary to acknowledge that they were children of wrath, and most unworthy of the least benefit of God. This place of Scripture therefore does not prove either that predestination and reprobation proceed from some cause holding itself on the part of men, or that God is to be argued an acceptor of persons.
pass_b_english: Further: in electing or passing by he regards no external circumstance of nation, nobility, or the like, but acts from the mere good pleasure of his will. Finally, those he passes by cannot pretend they feared God and lived justly; they are compelled instead to acknowledge they were children of wrath, most unworthy of the least divine benefit. So this Scripture place proves neither that predestination and reprobation proceed from some cause holding on the human side, nor that God is to be charged as an acceptor of persons.
source_text: Porro, in eligendo aut praetereundo non respicit aliquam externam circumstantiam gentis, nobilitatis, aut quid consimile, sed agit ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae. Denique, ii quos praeterit non possunt obtendere se Deum timuisse et juste vixisse, sed coguntur e contra agnoscere se fuisse irae filios, et minimo Dei beneficio indignissimos. Hic igitur locus Scripturae non probat, aut praedestinationem et reprobationem procedere ex causa aliqua se tenente ex parte hominum, aut Deum personarum acceptorem esse arguendum.
